lines.text: Nobody touched your money.
So why is it shrinking?
Follow the leak, and you'll find a three-hundred-year-old idea:
the Cantillon Effect.
In 1720, Paris was printing paper money like crazy.
lines.say: In seventeen-twenty, Paris was printing paper money like crazy.

lines.text: A banker named Richard Cantillon got rich from it...
lines.say: A banker named Richard [Cantillon](/kˌɑntijˈOn/) got rich from it...

lines.text: and then figured out why.
New money never reaches everyone at once.
It pours in at one spot... and flows down the line.
Whoever gets it first can spend it at today's prices.
But all that spending pushes prices up.
So the next person gets the money... after things already cost more.
By the time it reaches the end of the line, usually your paycheck, prices have already climbed.
Same money. Less stuff.
Today, new money mostly enters through banks and financial markets.
So stocks and homes tend to rise first... and wages, last.
Own assets? You ride the wave. Don't? You chase it.
Nobody stole anything.
The winners just stand closer to the tap.
So whenever new money appears, ask one question:
Who gets it first?
